stages.name: Business objectives: profit maximisation
stages.title: Business objectives: profit maximisation
stages.sub: Why firms aim to maximise profit, how the MC=MR rule finds that point, and three reasons this goal can cause problems.

steps.q: Economists usually assume people and firms make the best decisions they can with the information they have. If a firm owner wants as much money as possible from the business, what would they try to do with output and price?
steps.right: Pick whatever output makes profit as large as possible
steps.wrong: Pick whatever output makes revenue as large as possible
steps.hint: Profit is revenue minus cost, not revenue alone. Which one matches wanting the most money?

steps.q: A firm is making its 20th unit. Making it adds £8 to cost but adds £15 to revenue. Should the firm make that unit if it wants the biggest possible profit?
steps.right: Yes, that unit adds more to profit
steps.wrong: No, making any extra unit adds to cost
steps.hint: Compare what the unit adds to revenue against what it adds to cost.

steps.q: Now the firm is making its 40th unit. Making it adds £14 to cost but only £9 to revenue. Should the firm make that unit?
steps.wrong: Yes, more output always means more profit
steps.hint: Compare the extra revenue from this unit to the extra cost of making it.
steps.pre: Whenever the extra cost of one more unit is above the extra revenue, output is

steps.q: Below a certain output extra units add more revenue than cost, above it they add more cost than revenue. At the output in between, the extra revenue and extra cost of the last unit are exactly equal. What is true of profit at that exact output?
steps.right: Profit is as high as it can possibly be
steps.wrong: Profit is still rising with each unit
steps.hint: Just before this point extra units help profit, just after they hurt it. What must be true right at the point where they switch over?

steps.q: A firm cuts spending on new equipment and staff training to hit this year's biggest possible profit figure. Competitors keep investing. Five years on, who is likely to have the better technology and skills?
steps.wrong: The firm that maximised this year's profit
steps.hint: Squeezing out short-run profit often means spending less on things that only pay off later.
steps.pre: So chasing the biggest profit right now can

steps.q: To raise this year's profit further, a firm cuts staff wages, pays suppliers late and pollutes a nearby river to save on waste disposal. Besides the shareholders, who else is affected by this decision?
steps.right: Workers, suppliers and the local community
steps.wrong: Nobody else, only shareholders are affected
steps.hint: Profit maximisation focuses on one group's gain. Who else has an interest in how the firm behaves?
steps.pre: So profit maximisation can come at the expense of other

steps.q: The owners of a large company want maximum profit, but the salaried managers running it day to day care more about a bigger office, a larger team and an easier working life. Will the managers' choices necessarily match what the owners want?
steps.right: No, the managers may choose differently
steps.wrong: Yes, managers always act exactly as owners want
steps.hint: The people making decisions are not the people who own the profit. Do their interests have to line up?
steps.pre: This gap between owners' goals and the managers acting for them is the

steps.q: So even though the MC=MR rule shows the output that would maximise profit, is it guaranteed that a manager running the firm will actually choose that output?
steps.right: No, the manager may pursue other goals instead
steps.wrong: Yes, managers always pick the profit-maximising output
steps.hint: Think about whose interests the manager is actually acting on.
